problem: Psychological-test-style evaluations of LMs show general abilities but do not show whether a model uses those capabilities in a real task. Navigation instruction generators perform far below humans, and it is unclear whether search or pragmatic reasoning is the cause.
motivation: To align language models with humans, one needs task-specific diagnostics that point to which capability to improve. Humans generate instructions by sampling a few candidates and simulating the listener (Bayesian, Monte-Carlo-like reasoning), and the same structure can describe LMs and allow a human-vs-model comparison.
key_idea: Model both humans and LMs as bounded pragmatic speakers (base speaker generating candidates + theory-of-mind listener ranking them), quantify search and pragmatic deficiencies via oracle-substitution performance gains, and fix the pragmatic deficit with ensembles of simulated instruction-following listeners.
insight: The oracle analysis shows the pragmatic capability is the bottleneck: oracle search adds only ~9.4% on average, while a human as the ranker nearly doubles performance and even slightly exceeds human speakers' NDTW, so the search capability is already adequate. Ensembles of listeners beat single listeners (a single VLN-BERT hurts LSTM/Transformer speakers by 5.5/3.2 NDTW), and the agreement table shows listener-human agreement drops on model-generated instructions (covariate shift), so listeners trained only on human instructions are suboptimal ToM models.
method: Bounded pragmatic speaker: samples N candidates from base speaker S(u|τ) and picks argmax of the ToM listener score L(τ*|u), a Monte-Carlo approximation of the pragmatic speaker
Capability definitions: search = candidate set contains the optimal human instruction u*; pragmatic = ToM listener ranks u* first

Oracle-based evaluation (PPG): r*_search uses a gold candidate set containing the human reference; r*_pragmatic ranks the model's candidates with a real human listener; PPG = performance gap versus the original speaker

LMs cast as bounded pragmatic speakers: the candidate set is the decoded output plus N samples, with S used as both base speaker and ToM listener, under a better-than-sampling assumption (γ≈0.7–0.9 for N=10)

Augmented ToM listener: ensemble of K=10 instruction-following agents (EnvDrop or Recurrent VLN-BERT), each trained on a random 90% subset with different seeds, executed M times in the simulator; score = mean trajectory similarity Ψ (soft metric) to the intended path
Speakers: fine-tuned GPT-2 (decoder-only), LSTM encoder-decoder, Transformer encoder-decoder, trained by MLE on R2R
Human evaluation: MTurk PanGEA interface, 75 seen-val paths per system, 1,200 annotated instructions, 213 evaluators

setting.backbone: GPT-2 (fine-tuned), LSTM enc-dec, Transformer enc-dec speakers; ToM listeners are ensembles of 10 EnvDrop / Recurrent VLN-BERT / single VLN-BERT (trained)
setting.training_data: R2R train set (61 envs, 4,675 paths, ~3 instructions each); listeners trained on R2R human instructions; no extra data
setting.observation: Matterport3D panoramic RGB (36 views per step; ResNet-152 or CLIP features) plus orientation features
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (adjacent-location moves), speaker outputs text instructions
setting.privileged: Intended ground-truth trajectory given to the speaker (the task); simulator access for listener rollouts; oracle variants use human listener/reference instructions but the main method does not

numbers_note: This is an instruction-generation paper evaluated by real humans, not a standard navigation benchmark. Main Fig. 2 numbers appear only in figures. Table 2 values are NDTW only; the appendix table gives the full metrics for a subset of the configurations.
results: Adding an ensemble of 10 EnvDrop listeners as the ToM model raises the Transformer enc-dec speaker from 49.4 to 57.3 NDTW (+7.9). Recurrent VLN-BERT ensembles raise the LSTM speaker from 45.3 to 56.4 (+11.1). The abstract reports an 11% SR boost for guiding real humans, though the SR figure in the appendix table (LSTM 49.3→54.7) is smaller. A gap to humans remains (71.0–76.2 NDTW).
limitations: Single human per instruction, small MTurk population and 75 paths, so human-evaluation variance is not measured; humans may guess paths
Requires a simulator of the environment for listener rollouts, and relies on hypothetical cognitive models; validated only on R2R in Matterport3D
Listeners trained on human instructions suffer covariate shift on model-generated instructions; the remaining gap is not closed
builds_on: Rational Speech Acts / pragmatic speaker models
